farraa:1-1.t:
His saying: ﴿تِلْكَ آيَاتُ ٱلْقُرْآنِ وَكِتَابٍ مُّبِينٍ﴾: ﴿وكتابٍ مُبين﴾ is genitive; He means: and the verses of a clear Book. Had it been read ﴿وكتابٌ مبينٌ﴾, by referring it back to "the verses" [i.e. in the nominative], He would mean: and that is a clear Book. And if it were accusative as praise (ʿalā al-madḥ) — as one says: "I passed by a handsome man, and a tall, strapping one (wa-ṭawīlan sharmaḥan)" — that is a valid way. Praise is like his saying:
إلى الملِك القَرْم وابنِ الهُمَام * وليْثَ الكَتيِبة فى المزدَحَمْ
(To the king, the chief, son of the valiant lord — and the lion of the squadron in the press of battle.)
In praise, both its definite and its indefinite are put in the accusative.

farraa:2-2.t: His saying: ﴿هُدًى وَبُشْرَىٰ﴾ is nominative, and if you wish you may put it in the accusative. The accusative is by severance (ʿalā al-qaṭʿ, i.e. as a ḥāl), and the nominative is by a new beginning (istiʾnāf). Similar to it in al-Baqara: ﴿هُدًى للمتَّقِين﴾; and in Luqmān: ﴿هُدىً ورَحْمَةً لِلمُحْسِنِين﴾ is like it.

farraa:7-7.t: His saying: ﴿أَوْ آتِيكُمْ بِشِهَابٍ قَبَسٍ﴾: ʿĀṣim and al-Aʿmash put tanwīn on al-shihāb and al-qabas, and the people of Medina made it a genitive construct: (بشهابِ قَبَسٍ). This is like His saying ﴿وَلَدَارُ الآخِرَةِ﴾: of the kind in which a thing is annexed to its own name when its names differ.

farraa:8-8.t: His saying: ﴿نُودِيَ أَن بُورِكَ مَن فِي ٱلنَّارِ﴾: You make (أَنْ) in the position of the accusative if you take the name of Mūsā as latent in ﴿نُودى﴾; and if you do not take the name of Mūsā as latent, (أن) is in the position of the nominative: "that was called out". In the reading (ḥarf) of Ubayy: (أَنْ بُورِكتِ النارُ) ("that the fire has been blessed"). ﴿وَمَنْ حَوْلَهَا﴾ means the angels. The Arabs say: bārakaka Allāh, bāraka fīka and bāraka ʿalayka (may Allah bless you).

farraa:9-9.t: His saying: ﴿إِنَّهُ أَنَا ٱللَّهُ﴾: this hāʾ is the hāʾ of ʿimād (the support pronoun, i.e. the pronoun of the matter). It is a noun that does not appear [as a referent]. It has already been explained.

farraa:10-11.t:
His saying: ﴿كَأَنَّهَا جَآنٌّ﴾: al-jānn is the snake that is neither large nor small. His saying: ﴿وَلَّىٰ مُدْبِراً وَلَمْ يُعَقِّبْ﴾: he did not turn round.
His saying: ﴿إِنِّي لاَ يَخَافُ لَدَيَّ ٱلْمُرْسَلُونَ﴾; then He made an exception, saying: ﴿إَلاَّ مَن ظَلَمَ ثُمَّ بَدَّلَ حُسْناً بَعْدَ سُوۤءٍ﴾ — so this one is forgiven. Someone may say: how was he made one who fears? I say: there are two views on this. One is that you say: the messengers are protected (maʿṣūma), forgiven and safe on the Day of Resurrection, while whoever has mixed a righteous deed with another evil one fears and hopes; that is one view. The other is that you make the exception from those left out of the statement, because the meaning is: the messengers do not fear; fear is only for others than them.
Then He made the exception, saying: except whoever did wrong — for this one does not fear. He means: he was an idolater, then repented and did good, so that one is forgiven, not fearful.
Some grammarians have said that (إلا) in the language is equivalent to wāw (and), and that the meaning of this verse is: the messengers do not fear in My presence, nor does whoever did wrong and then substituted good. They made similar to it the saying of Allah: ﴿لِئَلاّ يَكُونَ لِلناسِ عَلَيْكمْ حُجَّةٌ إلاّ الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا﴾, i.e. "nor those who did wrong". I have not found that Arabic tolerates what they said, because I do not allow "The people stood except ʿAbd Allāh" while he is standing; exception is only that the noun after illā is taken out of the meaning of the nouns before illā. I do consider it permissible to say "You owe a thousand besides (siwā) another thousand"; if you put (إلاّ) in this position it is sound, and (إلاّ) then has the interpretation they gave. But [illā] on its own [135/b], where a small part is excepted from a large whole — no. Rather, what is like it is that which comes in the meaning of illā, like the meaning of the wāw, without being it [Translator's note: the source has «الولو», evidently for «الواو»].
His saying: ﴿خَالِدِين فِيهَا ما دَامَتِ السَّموَاتُ والأرْضُ إلاّ مَا شَاءَ رَبُّكَ﴾: in meaning it is "except (i.e. besides) what your Lord wills of increase". So do not make illā equivalent to the wāw, but equivalent to siwā (besides). When siwā is in the position of illā, it is sound in the meaning of the wāw, because you say "I have much wealth besides this", i.e. and this too I have — as though you said: I have much wealth, and this. It is more effective with siwā than with illā, because you may say "I have besides this (siwā hādhā)", but you do not say "illā hādhā".

farraa:12-12.t:
His saying: ﴿واضْمُم يَدَكَ فِي جَيْبِكَ تَخْرُجْ بَيْضَآءَ مِنْ غَيْرِ سُوۤءٍ فِي تِسْعِ آيَاتٍ﴾: its meaning is: do this, and it is a sign among nine. Then He said ﴿إِلَىٰ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾ and did not say "sent" or "dispatched", because his affair is known: that he was sent to Pharaoh. The poet said:
رأتنى بحبليها فصَدَّت مخافةً * وفى الحبل رَوْعاء الفؤاد فَرُوق
(She saw me with her two ropes and shied away in fear; and on the rope was a skittish-hearted, timid one.)
He meant: she saw me coming with her two ropes — with the two ropes of the she-camel — so he left a verb implied, as though he said: she saw me approaching.
His saying ﴿وَإلَى ثَمودَ أَخَاهُمْ صَالحاً﴾: accusative by an implied ﴿أرسلنا﴾ (We sent).

farraa:14-14.t: His saying: ﴿وَجَحَدُواْ بِهَا وَٱسْتَيْقَنَتْهَآ أَنفُسُهُمْ ظُلْماً وَعُلُوّاً﴾: he says: they denied the nine signs after their souls had become certain that they were from Allah, out of wrongdoing and arrogance. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: (ظلماً عُليّاً), like His saying ﴿وَقَدْ بَلَغْتُ مِنَ الكِبَر عُتيّاً﴾ and ﴿عِتِيّا﴾.

farraa:16-16.t:
His saying: ﴿وَوَرِثَ سُلَيْمَانُ دَاوُودَ﴾: Dāwūd had — according to what they mention — nineteen male children; Sulaymān was singled out for the inheritance only because it was the inheritance of kingship.
His saying ﴿عُلِّمْنَا مَنطِقَ ٱلطَّيْرِ﴾: the meaning of the speech of the birds; He made it like a man's speech since it was understood. The poet said:
عجبت لَهَا أنَّى يكُون غِناؤها * رَفيعاً ولم تَفتح بمنطقهَا فما
(I marvelled at her: how could her singing be so lofty, when she did not open a mouth for her speech?)
The poet made it like speech since he took it that she was weeping.

farraa:17-17.t: His saying: ﴿وَحُشِرَ لِسْلَيْمَانَ جُنُودُهُ مِنَ ٱلْجِنِّ وَٱلإِنْس وَٱلطَّيْرِ فَهُمْ يُوزَعُونَ﴾: these kinds used to be with Sulaymān when he rode out. ﴿فَهُمْ يُوزَعُونَ﴾: the first of them were held back for the last of them until they gathered together. It is from wazaʿtu al-rajul (I restrained the man); you say: "I shall surely restrain you (la-azaʿannakum) from wrongdoing", and this is from that.

farraa:19-19.t: As for His saying: ﴿أَوْزِعْنِيۤ﴾, its meaning is: inspire me.

farraa:22-22.t:
His saying: ﴿فَمَكَثَ غَيْرَ بَعِيدٍ﴾: the people read it with ḍamma [makutha], and ʿĀṣim read it with fatḥa: fa-makatha. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is (فتمكَّث). The meaning of ﴿غَيْرَ بَعِيدٍ﴾ is: not long in staying; "distant" and "long" are close [in meaning].
His saying ﴿فَقَالَ أَحَطتُ بِمَا لَمْ تُحِطْ بِهِ وَجِئْتُكَ﴾: some of the Arabs said aḥaṭṭu, putting the ṭāʾ in place of the tāʾ. When ṭāʾ meets tāʾ and the ṭāʾ before it is vowelless, the Arabs turn the ṭāʾ into tāʾ and say aḥattu, just as they turn the ẓāʾ into tāʾ in His saying ﴿أَوَعَتَّ أَمْ لَمْ تَكُنْ مِنَ الواعِظِينَ﴾, and the dhāl and the dāl into tāʾ, as in ﴿أَخَتُّمْ﴾ — I saw it in some of the copies of ʿAbd Allāh as (وأَخَتُّمْ). And some of the Arabs turn the tāʾ, when it comes after the ṭāʾ, into ṭāʾ and say: aḥaṭṭ.
His saying ﴿وجئْتُكَ مِنْ سبَأ بِنَبإٍ يَقِينٍ﴾: the readers treat ﴿سَبأ﴾ as fully declinable (ijrāʾ), because — according to what they mention — it is a man; likewise make it declinable if it is the name of a mountain. Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ did not make it declinable. Al-Ruʾāsī claimed he asked Abū ʿAmr about it and he said: I do not know what it is. He took a [reasonable] position, since he did not know what it was, because when the Arabs name [something] with an unknown name they leave it undeclined, as al-Aʿshā said:
وتدفنُ منه الصَّالحاتُ وإن يُسئْ * يكن ما أساء النارَ فى رأس كَبْكَبا
(His good deeds are buried, while if he does ill, his ill becomes a fire on the top of Kabkab.)
[136/a] It is as though he did not know Kabkab. I heard Abū al-Saffāḥ al-Salūlī say: "This is Abū Ṣuʿrūr, he has come," and he did not decline it, because it is not in their custom of naming.
Al-Farrāʾ said: al-ṣuʿrūr is something like gum.
The poet said, not declining it:
الواردون وتيم فى ذُرَا سَبَأٍ * قد عضّ أعْنَاقَهم جلدُ الجواميسِ
(Those who come down to water, and Taym, in the heights of Sabaʾ — the hide of buffaloes has bitten into their necks.)
[Translator's note: in the verse as given here سَبَأٍ carries tanwīn, though it is cited for non-declension.] And if you made it the name of the tribe, if it is a man, or the name of what is around it, if it is a mountain, you would not make it declinable either.

farraa:25-25.t:
His saying: ﴿أَلاَّ يَسْجُدُواْ للَّهِ﴾: It is read ﴿أَلاَّ يَسْجُدُواْ﴾, with ﴿يَسجْدوا﴾ in the position of the accusative; so Ḥamza read it. Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī, al-Ḥasan and Ḥumayd al-Aʿraj read it without doubling: (ألاَ يَسْجُدُوا), in the sense of "Lo! O you, prostrate!": "you" (hāʾulāʾ) is implied, and (يا) alone suffices for it. He said: I heard some of the Arabs say: "alā yā irḥamānā, alā yā taṣaddaqā ʿalaynā" (Lo! O, have mercy on us both; Lo! O, give alms to us both). He said: he meant me and my companion. The poet — al-Akhṭal — said:
أَلاَ يا اسلمى يا هند هندَ بنى بَدْر * وإن كان حَيَّاناَ عِدىً آخِر الدهر
(Lo! O be safe, O Hind, Hind of Banū Badr, even if our two clans are enemies to the end of time.)
Abū al-ʿAbbās related to us: Muḥammad related to us: al-Farrāʾ related to us: one of the shaykhs — namely al-Kisāʾī — related to me from ʿĪsā al-Hamdānī, who said: I never heard the shaykhs read it except without doubling, intending the imperative. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is (هَلاّ تسجدونَ لله) with tāʾ, and this is evidence for whoever reads it without doubling. In the reading of Ubayy: (أَلاَ تسجدونَ لله الذى يعلم سِرَّكم ومَا تَعلِنُون), and that is the proper sense of the passage, because it is a prostration [verse]. Whoever reads ﴿أَلاَّ يَسْجُدُوا﴾ with doubling, it ought not to be a prostration [verse], because the meaning is: Satan made it fair-seeming to them that they should not prostrate; and Allah knows best about that.
His saying ﴿يُخْرِجُ ٱلْخَبْءَ﴾ is with hamza. It is the unseen: the unseen of the heavens and the unseen of the earth. It is also said: it is the water that comes down from the sky and the vegetation from the earth. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: (يخرج الخَبْءَ منَ السَّواتِ) [Translator's note: so in the source, for السموات]. (فى) is sound in place of (من) because you say "I shall surely extract from you the knowledge that is in you", and then you omit whichever of the two you wish — I mean (من) and (فى) — and the meaning remains as it is.

farraa:28-28.t: His saying: ﴿ثُمَّ تَوَلَّ عَنْهُمْ فَٱنْظُرْ﴾: Someone may say: how did he order it to turn away from them, when he said ﴿فانْظُرْ مَاذَا يَرْجِعُونَ﴾? That is clear in Arabic: he urged it on, saying: "Go with this letter of mine and hurry"; then ﴿فانظر ماذا يَرجعونَ﴾ was placed later, while its meaning is placed earlier. It is also said that he ordered the hoopoe to drop the letter and then hide from her, and it did so: it dropped the letter and flew to an opening in the wall of her council chamber. Allah knows best what is correct in that.

farraa:29-29.t: His saying: ﴿إِنِّيۤ أُلْقِيَ إِلَيَّ كِتَابٌ كَرِيمٌ﴾: she called it noble because it was sealed; so I was told. It is also said: she described the letter as noble to her people because she saw the letter of a king with her, so she called it noble for the nobility of its sender. It is also said that she said (كريم) before she knew that it was from Sulaymān. That does not please me, because she was literate and had read the letter before going out to her council.

farraa:30-30.t: His saying: ﴿إِنَّهُ مِن سُلَيْمَانَ وَإِنَّهُ بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ ٱلرَّحْمَـٰنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ﴾: both are with kasra, I mean inna and inna. Had both been with fatḥa it would be permissible, according to your saying: "it was cast to me that it is from Sulaymān and that it is: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate." Their position is then nominative, by repetition (takrīr, i.e. substitution) for "the letter": "it was cast to me that it is from Sulaymān". And if you wish, they are in the position of the accusative because of the dropping of the preposition from them. In the reading of Ubayy: (وأَنْ بِسمِ الله الرحمن الرحيم), and that is evidence for whoever reads both with fatḥa, because (أَن), when its alif is with fatḥa with a verb or with what is quoted, can only be with the nūn lightened.

farraa:31-31.t: His saying: ﴿أَلاَّ تَعْلُواْ﴾: its alif is with fatḥa; kasra is not permissible. It is in the position of the nominative if you make it a repetition on ﴿أُلْقِى﴾, and accusative on [the sense]: "the letter was cast to me with this (bi-dhā)", and then you dropped the bāʾ and put it in the accusative. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: (وإنه من سليمان وإنه بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم), and this indicates the kasra, because it is conjoined to: "Indeed, it was cast to me", "and indeed it is from Sulaymān". In the reading of Ubayy, it may be that you make the (أَن) that is in "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" the same (أن) as in His saying ﴿أن لا تعلوا عَلىَّ﴾, as though in meaning: "it was cast to me: that you not exalt yourselves against me". When it was placed in (بسمِ الله), it was repeated in its position in ﴿أن لا تعلوا﴾, just as Allah said: ﴿أَيَعِدُكُمْ أَنّكُمْ إذا مِتُّمْ وَكُنْتُمْ تُرَاباً وعِظَاماً أَنَّكُمْ﴾ — "annakum" is repeated and its meaning is one, and Allah knows best. Do you not see that the meaning is: does he promise you that you will be brought out when you have become dust and bones?

farraa:32-32.t:
His saying: ﴿يٰأَيُّهَا ٱلْمَلأُ أَفْتُونِي﴾: she made consultation a fatwā (legal opinion). That is permissible because of the breadth of Arabic.
His saying ﴿مَا كُنتُ قَاطِعَةً أَمْراً﴾: in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: (ما كنتُ قاضيةً أمراً), and the meaning is the same. You say: I do not decide (lā aqṭaʿu) a matter without you, and I do not settle (lā aqḍī) a matter without you.

farraa:34-34.t: His saying: ﴿قَالَتْ إِنَّ ٱلْمُلُوكَ إِذَا دَخَلُواْ قَرْيَةً﴾ is an answer to their saying ﴿نَحْنُ أُولُو قُوَّةٍ وأولُو بأسٍ شَدِيدٍ﴾. She said: if they enter your land they will humiliate you, though you are kings. And Allah said: ﴿وَكَذٰلِكَ يَفْعَلُونَ﴾.

farraa:35-35.t:
His saying: ﴿وَإِنِّي مُرْسِلَةٌ إِلَيْهِمْ بِهَدِيَّةٍ فَنَاظِرَةٌ بِمَ يَرْجِعُ ٱلْمُرْسَلُونَ﴾: the alif is dropped from His saying (بم) because it means "with what thing will the envoys return?" When (مَا) is in the position of (أىّ, which?) and is then joined to a preposition that governs the genitive, the alif of (مَا) is dropped so that the interrogative is distinguished from the statement. Of this kind is His saying ﴿فِيمَ كُنْتم﴾ and ﴿عَمَّ يتساءَلُونَ﴾; and if you write it in full, that is correct. Al-Mufaḍḍal recited to me:
إنا قتلنا بقتلانا سَرَاتكم * أهلَ اللوَاء ففيما يكثر القِيلُ
(We have killed your chiefs, the bearers of the banner, for our slain; so over what is there so much talk?)
And al-Mufaḍḍal also recited to me:
على ما قام يشتمنَا لَئِيمٌ * كخنزير تمرَّغ فى رمَادِ
(Over what does a base man stand up to revile us, like a pig rolling in ashes?)
His saying: ﴿إِلَيْهِمْ بِهَدِيَّةٍ﴾ — she means Sulaymān — is like His saying ﴿عَلَى خَوْفٍ مِنْ فِرْعَوْنَ وَمَلَئِهمْ﴾. And she said ﴿بِمَ يَرْجِعُ المُرْسَلُونَ﴾, while her envoy — according to what they mention — was a single woman; she used the plural while it was only one envoy. That is why He said ﴿فلمَّا جَاءَ سُلَيْمانَ﴾, meaning: when the envoy came to Sulaymān. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: (فلما جَاءوا سليمان); since He said ﴿المرسَلونَ﴾, ﴿جَاءوا﴾ is sound [too], though the one sent was one. This is indicated by Sulaymān's saying ﴿ارْجِعْ إليْهِمْ﴾.

farraa:36-36.t:
His saying: ﴿أَتُمِدُّونَنِ بِمَالٍ﴾: in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is with two nūns and a written yāʾ. Ḥamza read it (أَتُمِدُّونَّى بمالٍ): he means the reading of ʿAbd Allāh, but he assimilated the nūn into the nūn and doubled it. ʿĀṣim ibn Abī al-Najūd read (أَتُمِدُّونَنِ بمالٍ) with two nūns without yāʾ. All are correct.
His saying: ﴿فَمَآ آتَانِيَ ٱللَّهُ﴾ — and he did not say ﴿فما آتانِىَ الله﴾ [Translator's note: so in the source; the contrast intended is evidently between the yāʾ-less written form آتانِ and the form with the yāʾ] — because it is written without the yāʾ in the text (al-kitāb). Whoever is among those who allow adding to the Quran the yāʾs and wāws that are dropped — as in His saying ﴿وَيَدْعُ الإنْسَان بالشَّرِّ﴾, where he writes in the wāw though it is not in the muṣḥaf, or [reads] al-munādī for al-munād — may say ﴿أتمدُّونَنِ﴾ with the yāʾ, and may vowel it [137/a] with the accusative fatḥa, as was said ﴿وَمَالِىَ لاَ أَعْبُدُ﴾; likewise ﴿فَمَا آتانِىَ الله﴾ is permissible. But I do not care for that, nor do I adopt it. Following the muṣḥaf, when I find a way for it in the speech of the Arabs and the reading of the readers, is dearer to me than departing from it. Abū ʿAmr used to read (إنَّ هَذَيْنِ لسَاحِرَان), and I do not dare to do that; and he read ﴿فَأَصَّدَّقَ وَأَكُونَ﴾, adding a wāw to the text, and I do not favour that.

farraa:37-37.t:
His saying: ﴿لاَّ قِبَلَ لَهُمْ بِهَا﴾: in the muṣḥaf of ʿAbd Allāh it is (لَهُمْ بهم), and it is the same.
His saying: ﴿ٱرْجِعْ إِلَيْهِمْ﴾: this is from Sulaymān's words to her envoy — he means [the envoy of] Bilqīs. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: (ارجعوا إليهم), and that is correct, according to what I explained to you about His saying ﴿يأيُّها النَّبىّ إذا طلَّقْتُمُ النِّسَاءَ﴾: addressing one person while meaning those with him, which occurs in much speech.

farraa:39-39.t: His saying: ﴿عِفْرِيتٌ مِّن ٱلْجِنِّ أَنَاْ آتِيكَ بِهِ﴾: al-ʿifrīt is the strong and effective one. Some of the Arabs say ʿifriya for ʿifrīt. Whoever says ʿifriya says in its plural ʿafārin; and whoever says ʿifrīt says ʿafārīt, and he may also say ʿafārin. In one of the two readings: (وَما أُهِلَّ بِهِ للطواغِى), meaning the plural of ṭāghūt. His saying ﴿أَنَا آتِيكَ بِهِ قَبْلَ أَنْ تَقُومَ مِنْ مَقَامِكَ﴾ means: before he rises from the seat of judgement; he used to sit until midday. He said: I want [something] quicker (than that).

farraa:40-40.t: His saying: ﴿قَالَ ٱلَّذِي عِندَهُ عِلْمٌ مِّنَ ٱلْكِتَابِ أَنَاْ آتِيكَ بِهِ قَبْلَ أَن يَرْتَدَّ إِلَيْكَ طَرْفُكَ﴾: he says: before the thing reaches you from the extent of your sight. Ibn ʿAbbās said about His saying (عِنْدهُ عِلْمٌ مِنَ الكتاب): ﴿يا حَىُّ يا قيُّوم﴾ ("O Ever-Living, O Self-Subsisting"). It is mentioned that her throne sank into the ground in its place and then sprang up at Sulaymān's seat.

farraa:41-41.t: As for His saying: ﴿نَكِّرُواْ لَهَا عَرْشَهَا﴾: he ordered them to enlarge it, in order to test her intelligence when she came. The devils had feared that Sulaymān would marry her, so they said: there is something [wrong] in her mind, and her leg is like the leg of a donkey. So Sulaymān ordered the throne to be changed for that reason, and ordered water, which was made to run beneath the glass pavilion (al-ṣarḥ), with fish in it. When she came, it was said to her: (أَهَكَذَا عَرْشُكِ). She recognised it and did not recognise it; she did not say "It is it", nor "It is not it", but said (كَأنَّه هُوَ). Then she lifted her garment from her shins, thinking she was walking into a lujja — a lujja is a great body of water — and he looked upon the most beautiful shins and feet. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: (وَكَشَفَ عَنْ رِجْليهَا) ("and she uncovered her feet").

farraa:43-43.t:
His saying: ﴿وَصَدَّهَا مَا كَانَت تَّعْبُدُ﴾: he says: she was intelligent; what kept her from the worship of Allah was only the worship of the sun and the moon, which was a custom of her forefathers' religion. The meaning of the passage: what she used to worship — i.e. her worship of the sun and moon — kept her from worshipping Allah. (ما) is in the position of the nominative. It has also been said: ﴿إن صدَّها﴾ [Translator's note: so in the source; read: «صدَّها»]: Sulaymān prevented her from what she used to worship; [then] the position of (ما) is accusative, because the verb belongs to Sulaymān. Some of them said: the verb belongs to Allah the Exalted: Allah kept her from what she used to worship.
His saying: ﴿إِنَّهَا كَانَتْ مِن قَوْمٍ كَافِرِينَ﴾: the alif has kasra, as a new beginning (istiʾnāf). And if a reader read ﴿أنَّها﴾, he would refer it back to the position of (ما) in its nominative: "that she was of a disbelieving people kept her from the worship of Allah". It is like your saying: "What I was engaged in kept me from visiting you — that I was going out early and coming back late": anna explains the meaning of "what I was engaged in".

farraa:45-45.t: His saying: ﴿فَرِيقَانِ يَخْتَصِمُونَ﴾: the meaning of ﴿يختصمُونَ﴾ is: differing — a believer and a denier.

farraa:47-47.t: His saying: ﴿قَالَ طَائِرُكُمْ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ﴾: he says: in the Preserved Tablet with Allah. You take me as an ill omen and augur ill of me, and all of that is from Allah. It is like His saying ﴿قالوا طَائِرُكُمْ مَعَكُمْ﴾, i.e. it is bound to you: whatever there is of good or evil is bound upon your necks. He has made it clear in His saying ﴿وَكُلَّ إنْسَانٍ ألْزَمْنَاهُ طَائِرَهُ فىعُنُقِهِ﴾.

farraa:49-49.t: His saying: ﴿قَالُواْ تَقَاسَمُواْ بِٱللَّهِ﴾: in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is (تقاسَمُوا بالله), without ﴿قالوا﴾. His saying: ﴿لَنُبَيِّتَنَّهُ﴾: tāʾ, nūn and yāʾ have all been read. Whoever says ﴿تقاسموا﴾ and makes ﴿تقاسموا﴾ a statement (khabar, i.e. a past verb), it is as though he said "swearing to one another": ﴿لَنُبَيِّتَنَّهُ﴾ with the nūn. Then the yāʾ is permissible with this meaning, so you say: they said ﴿ليبيتُنَّه﴾ with yāʾ, just as you say lanaqūmanna, layaqūmanna and layaqūmunna. Whoever says taqāsamū and makes it in the position of the jussive [i.e. an imperative], it is as though he said: "Make a pact and swear: you shall surely attack him by night (latubayyitunnahu)" with tāʾ. And the nūn is permissible in this respect, because the one who said to them "swear to one another" is included with them in the act, even though he commanded them; do you not see that you say "Stand up, let us go (nadhhab) to so-and-so", because he commands them while being with them in the act? The nūn is the most pleasing of the options to me. Al-Kisāʾī reads with tāʾ, and the generality [of readers] are on the nūn. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: (تقاسَمُوا) (ثم لنُقْسِمَنًّ ما شهِدْنَا مَهْلك أهله). Allah has said ﴿تَعَالَوا نَدْعُ أَبْنَاءَنا وأبْنَاءَكُمْ﴾, because they called them so that all of them should do together what they called them to. The people of Medina, ʿĀṣim and al-Ḥasan read it with the nūn, and the companions of ʿAbd Allāh with the tāʾ. Abū al-ʿAbbās related to us: Muḥammad related to us: al-Farrāʾ related to us: Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna related to me from Ḥumayd al-Aʿraj from Mujāhid that he read (ليُبَيِّتُنَّه) with the yāʾ.

farraa:51-51.t: His saying: ﴿فَٱنظُرْ كَيْفَ كَانَ عَاقِبَةُ مَكْرِهِمْ أَنَّا دَمَّرْنَاهُمْ﴾: It is read with kasra, as a new beginning (istiʾnāf), like His saying: ﴿فَلْيَنْظُرِ الإنسانُ إلَى طَعَامِهِ أنّا صَبَبْنَا الماءَ﴾: he begins anew while explaining by it what came before. And whoever refers it back to what came before [Translator's note: the source has «على إعلى», a scribal slip for «على»] says (أَنَّا) with fatḥa; then (أَنَّا) is in the position of the nominative, made to follow "the outcome" (al-ʿāqiba). And if you wish, you may make it accusative in two ways: one is to refer it to the position of (كيف); the other is to repeat (كان), as though you said: "the outcome of their plotting was Our destroying them". And if you wish, you may make it a single phrase and put (أَنَّا) in the position of the accusative, as though you said: "so look how the outcome of their plotting was: Our destroying them". And His saying: ﴿وأنتم تبصرونَ تعلمون أَن فاحشة﴾ [Translator's note: so in the source, apparently a fragment concerning 27:54].

farraa:59-59.t: His saying: ﴿قُلِ ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ وَسَلاَمٌ عَلَىٰ عِبَادِهِ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱصْطَفَىٰ﴾: It was said to Lūṭ: ﴿قُلِ ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ﴾ for the destruction of those who were destroyed, ﴿وَسَلاَمٌ عَلَىٰ عِبَادِهِ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱصْطَفَىٰ﴾. ﴿ءَآللَّهُ خَيْرٌ أَمَّا يُشْرِكُونَ﴾: he says: is the worship of Allah better, or the worship of idols?

farraa:60-60.t:
His saying: ﴿فَأَنبَتْنَا بِهِ حَدَآئِقَ ذَاتَ بَهْجَةٍ﴾: He said ﴿ذاتَ﴾ and did not say dhawāt, and each is correct. It is permissible to say ﴿ذات﴾ for "gardens", which is a plural, only because you say "these are gardens" just as you say "this is a garden". Similar is the saying of Allah ﴿وَلِلّهِ الأسْمَاءُ الحُسْنَى﴾, where He did not say al-ḥusan, and (والقُرون الأولَي). Had it been "gardens dhawāt bahja", it would be correct. Al-Aʿshā said, using the singular form:
فسوف يُعقبُنيهِ إن ظفرتَ به * ربٌّ غفورٌ وبِيض ذات أطهار
(A forgiving Lord will requite me for it, if you get hold of it, and fair women of purity.)
He did not say dhawāt aṭhār. Ḥadīqa is said only of every orchard that has a wall around it; what has no wall around it is not called ḥadīqa.
His saying: ﴿أَإِلَـٰهٌ مَّعَ ٱللَّهِ﴾ refers back to His saying ﴿أَمْ مَنْ خَلَق﴾ such-and-such. Then He said ﴿أَإِلَـٰهٌ مَّعَ ٱللَّهِ﴾ created it? And if you wish, you may make its nominative due to maʿa, as in your saying: "Is there with Allah — woe to you! — a god?" And it could come in the accusative, aʾilāhan maʿa Allāh, by implying a verb through which the accusative arises, as in your saying: "Do you set up a god with Allah?" or "Do you take a god with Allah?"
The Arabs say: "A fox, and you run away?!" (a-thaʿlaban wa-tafirru), as though they meant: "Do you see a fox and run away?" One of the poets said:
أَعبداً حلَّ فى شُعَبىَ غريباً * أَلُؤْماً لا أبالكَ واغترابَا
(A slave settling as a stranger in Shuʿabā? Baseness — may you have no father! — and being a stranger too?)
He means: do you combine baseness and estrangement? I heard one of the Arabs [speak] of a captive he had taken by night; when [138/a] morning came he saw that he was black, and said: "A slave, the whole night through!", as though he said: do I not see that I have captured a slave since my night [began]? Another said:
أجَخْفا تميميّاً إذا فتنة خَبَتْ * وجُبْناً إذا ما المشرفيّة سُلَّت
(Boastfulness, O Tamīmī, when strife has died down, and cowardice when the Mashrafī swords are drawn?)
This is in every [expression of] wonder in which they address the person concerned. But when one wonders at something while addressing someone else, they make the verb govern and say: "A fox, and a man running away from it!" [a-thaʿlabun wa-rajulun yafirru minhu], because this is addressed to someone other than the one with the fox. And if it were put in the accusative according to "Does a man run away from a fox?", you would make the conjoined as though it were the preceding element; it is built on this. I heard one of Banū ʿUqayl recite, by Majnūn of Banū ʿĀmir:
أألبرقَ أم نارا لليلى بدت لنَا * بمُنْخَرقٍ من سَارياتِ الجنائبِ
(Was it lightning, or a fire of Laylā, that appeared to us in a wind-swept tract of the night-travelling south winds?)
And he recited to me in it:
بل البرقَ يبدو فى ذَرَى دَفَئيَّة * يضىء نَشَاصاً مشمخرّ الغَوارب
(Nay, it was lightning appearing in the peaks of a spring cloud, lighting up towering cloud-masses with lofty crests.)
He put all of this in the accusative, with its verb accompanying it, by implying a verb of it, as though he said: do I see a fire? Nay, I see lightning. And as though he said: and if I [only] saw the fire of Laylā. Likewise the other two verses, in His saying ﴿أَإِلَـٰهٌ مَّعَ ٱللَّهِ﴾.

farraa:65-65.t: His saying: ﴿قُل لاَّ يَعْلَمُ مَن فِي ٱلسَّمَاواتِ وٱلأَرْضِ ٱلْغَيْبَ إِلاَّ ٱللَّهُ﴾: You put what comes after (إلاّ) in the nominative because in what precedes it there is a negation (jaḥd), and it [the preceding noun] is nominative. Had it been accusative it would be correct. In one of the two readings: ﴿مَا فعَلوهُ إلا قليلاً منهم﴾ in the accusative, and in our reading in the nominative; each is correct. This is when the negation before illā is with definite nouns. When it is with an indefinite, they say nothing but the following [construction] (itbāʿ) of what precedes (إلاّ); they say: "No one went except your father (abūka)", and they do not say "except abāka". That is because "the father" takes the place of "anyone": this is one and that is one, so they preferred itbāʿ. In the first case, what precedes (إلاَّ) is a plural and what follows (إلاّ) is one of it or part of it, not all of it.

farraa:66-66.t:
His saying: ﴿بَلِ ٱدَّارَكَ عِلْمُهُمْ فِي ٱلآخِرَةِ﴾: its meaning is: perhaps their knowledge has come in succession (tadāraka). He says: their knowledge of the Hereafter followed in succession; he means: with knowledge of the Hereafter, whether it will be or not. That is why He said ﴿بَلْ هُمْ فِي شَكٍّ مِّنْهَا بَلْ هُم مِّنْهَا عَمُونَ﴾. In the reading of Ubayy: (أَمْ تداركَ عِلمُهُم فى الآخرة) with am. The Arabs put (بل) in place of (أم) and (أم) in place of (بل) when there is an interrogative at the beginning of the speech, as in the poet's saying:
فواالله ما أجرِى أسَلْمَى تَغَوَّلتْ * أم النومُ أم كلّ إلى حَبِيبُ
(By Allah, I do not know: has Salmā changed like a ghoul, or is it sleep, or are all dear to me?)
Their meaning is: bal (nay rather). The readers differed over ﴿ادّارك﴾: Yaḥyā, al-Ḥasan, Shayba and Nāfiʿ read (بل ادَّاركَ); and Mujāhid [and] Abū Jaʿfar al-Madanī read (بَلْ أَدْرَكَ عِلْمُهُمْ فِى الآخِرة), from adraktu (I attained), and its meaning is as though he said: has their knowledge attained the knowledge of the Hereafter? It has reached me from Ibn ʿAbbās that he read (بَلَى أَدَّارك), as a question, doubling the dāl and putting a yāʾ in (بلى). That is a good reading, because it is more like mockery of the deniers, as in your saying to a man you are calling a liar: "Yes indeed (balā), by my life, you have met the predecessors, so you relate what we do not relate!" — while you are calling him a liar.

farraa:67-67.t: His saying: ﴿أَإِنَّا لَمُخْرَجُونَ﴾ and ﴿إنَّنَا﴾: in the copies of the people of Syria it is ﴿إنَّنَا﴾.

farraa:72-72.t:
His saying: ﴿قُلْ عَسَىٰ أَن يَكُونَ رَدِفَ لَكُم بَعْضُ ٱلَّذِي تَسْتَعْجِلُونَ﴾: It has come in the exegesis: "some of what you seek to hasten has drawn near to you". It is as though the lām came in because the meaning is "drew near", as the poet said: [138/a]
فقلت لها الحاجَاتُ يطرحن بالفتى * وهمٌّ تعَنّانى مُعَنّىً ركائبُهُ
(I said to her: needs fling a young man about, and a care has wearied me whose mounts are themselves wearied.)
He put the bāʾ on "the young man" because the meaning of ﴿يَطرحن﴾ is "they throw", and you say "I threw [with] the thing (ramaytu bi-l-shayʾ)" and "I flung it". The lām may be intrusive, the meaning being "radifakum" (has followed you), just as some of the Arabs said: "nafadhtu lahā miʾatan", meaning "nafadhtuhā miʾatan" (I paid her a hundred).

farraa:76-76.t: His saying: ﴿إِنَّ هَـٰذَا ٱلْقُرْآنَ يَقُصُّ عَلَىٰ بَنِيۤ إِسْرَائِيلَ أَكْثَرَ ٱلَّذِي هُمْ فِيهِ يَخْتَلِفُونَ﴾: That is because the Children of Israel differed until some of them cursed others, so Allah said: this Quran relates to them the guidance concerning what they differed over, if they would take it.

farraa:81-81.t:
His saying: ﴿وَمَآ أَنتَ بِهَادِي ٱلْعُمْيِ عَن ضَلالَتِهِمْ﴾: Had you said bi-hādin al-ʿumya [with tanwīn and the accusative], it would be correct. Ḥamza read (ومَا أنتَ تَهْدِى العُمْى عَن ضَلاَلتِهم), because in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is (وما إن تهدى العمى), which are two negatives combined, as the poet — Durayd ibn al-Ṣimma — said:
ما إن رَأيْتُ ولا سَمعتُ به * كاليوم طالِى أينْقُ جُرْبِ
(I have never seen nor heard of anyone like today's tar-smearer of mangy she-camels.)

farraa:82-82.t: His saying: ﴿وَإِذَا وَقَعَ ٱلْقَوْلُ عَلَيْهِم﴾: its meaning is: when wrath becomes due upon them. It is like His saying ﴿حَقَّ عليهم القَوْلُ﴾ in another place. His saying ﴿أَخْرَجْنَا لَهُمْ دَآبَّةً مِّنَ ٱلأَرْضِ تُكَلِّمُهُمْ﴾: the readers agree on the doubling of ﴿تكلّمهم﴾, and it is from speech (al-kalām). One of the ḥadīth transmitters told me that he said ﴿تُكَلِّمُهُمْ﴾ and ﴿تَكْلِمُهم﴾ ("it will wound them"). His saying (أَنَّ ٱلنَّاسَ) is read with fatḥa and with kasra. Whoever reads it with fatḥa makes the speaking fall upon it: ﴿تُكَلِّمُهُمْ بأَنَّ ٱلنَّاسَ﴾, and its position is accusative. In the reading (ḥarf) of ʿAbd Allāh: ﴿بأن الناس﴾, and in the reading of Ubayy: (تُنَبِّئهم أنّ الناسَ); these two are evidence for whoever reads it with fatḥa. The people of Medina [read] ﴿تُكَلِّمُهُمْ إِنَّ ٱلنَّاسَ﴾, so (إنَّ) is a new statement, yet it carries the meaning of the speech falling [on it]. Similar is ﴿فَلْيَنْظُرِ الإنْسانُ إلى طعَامِهِ﴾: whoever says (أَنَّا) makes it genitive, referred back to "food": "to [the fact] that We poured down water"; and whoever reads it with kasra says: innā — He informed [them] of the cause of the food, how Allah decreed it.

farraa:87-87.t:
His saying: ﴿وَيَوْمَ يُنفَخُ فِي ٱلصُّورِ فَفَزِعَ﴾: He did not say fa-yafzaʿu; He made faʿala (the past) refer back to yafʿalu (the imperfect). That is because in meaning it is: "and when the trumpet is blown, then [they] are terrified". Do you not see that your saying "I will stand on the day you stand" is like your saying "I will stand when you stand"? So it was answered with faʿala, because faʿala and yafʿalu are both sound with idhā. If you say: then where is the answer to His saying ﴿وَيَوْمَ يُنفَخُ فِي ٱلصُّورِ﴾? I say: it may be in an implied faʿala with the wāw, as though He said: "and that is the day the trumpet is blown". And if you wish, you may say: its answer is left out, as He said ﴿وَلَوْ تَرَى إذ فَزِعُوا فَلاَ فَوْتَ﴾.
And His saying: ﴿وَلَوْ يَرَى الذِينَ ظَلَموا﴾: its answer has been left out. And Allah knows best.
His saying ﴿وَكُلٌّ أَتَوْهُ دَاخِرِينَ﴾: the readers lengthen the alif [ātūhu], meaning: "fāʿilūhu" (coming to Him). Ḥamza shortened it. Abū al-ʿAbbās related to us: Muḥammad related to us: al-Farrāʾ related to us: a number of people related to me, among them al-Mufaḍḍal al-Ḍabbī, Qays and Abū Bakr, all of them from Jaḥsh ibn Ziyād al-Ḍabbī, from Tamīm ibn Ḥadhlam, who said: I recited to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd (وَكُلٌّ آتَوْهُ دَاخِرِينَ) with the alif lengthened, and he said: ﴿وَكُلٌّ أَتَوْهُ﴾ without lengthening the alif. It is a good reading, referred back to His saying ﴿فَفَزِع﴾, as you say in ordinary speech: "he saw me and was terrified, and came back abased". Referring faʿala to its like is more pleasing to me, together with the reading of ʿAbd Allāh. Abū al-ʿAbbās related to us: Muḥammad related to us: al-Farrāʾ related to us, saying: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Idrīs related to me from al-Aʿmash from Tamīm from ʿAbd Allāh the like of the report of Abū Bakr and his companions.

farraa:89-89.t: His saying: ﴿وَهُمْ مِّن فَزَعٍ يَوْمَئِذٍ آمِنُونَ﴾: The reading of the readers is with the genitive construct; they said ﴿وَهُمْ مِّن فَزَعٍ يَوْمَئِذٍ﴾ and ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ﴾ [Translator's note: the two forms are identical in the source as printed; the intended contrast is evidently between fazaʿi yawmiʾidhin and yawmaʾidhin]. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd read, in a chain of transmission part of which is part of what I related to you: (مِّن فَزَعٍ يَوْمَئِذٍ); Tamīm recited it to them thus: (وَهُمْ من فَزَعٍ يَوْمِئذٍ), and he [Ibn Masʿūd] took it with tanwīn and the accusative. The genitive construct is more pleasing to me — even though I read with the accusative — because it is a known terror; do you not see that He said (لاَ يَحْزُنُهُمْ الفَزَعُ الأَكْبَرُ) and made it [139/a] definite? So annexing it, so that it becomes definite, is more pleasing to me. And it is correct.

farraa:92-92.t: His saying: ﴿وَأَنْ أَتْلُوَ ٱلْقُرْآنَ﴾: In one of the two readings: (وَأَنِ اتْلُ), without the wāw, in the jussive as a command. The wāw has been dropped from it because of the jussive as a command, as He said ﴿قُلْ إنّى أُمِرْت أَنْ أَكُون أَوَّلَ مَنْ أَسْلَمَ وَلاَ تَكُونَنَّ﴾: He made the wāw, with the prohibition, refer back to a word put in the accusative by an, because the meaning comes with (أمرت) in both ways together. Do you not see that you say: "I ordered ʿAbd Allāh that he should stand (an yaqūma)" and "that: stand! (wa-an qum)"? Allah said ﴿وَأُمِرْنَا لِنُسْلِمَ لِرَبِّ الْعَالمينَ وَأَنْ أَقِيمُوا الصَّلاَة﴾, and this is like His saying ﴿وَأَنْ أَتْلُو القرآنَ﴾.
